## Proof

We wish to determine
$$\max_{a,\,b\,\in\,U(V)} N(a-b), \qquad N(a):=\max_{|v|=1}|av|.$$

Here $V$ is a finite-dimensional complex inner product space, $U(V)$ is the unitary group, and $N$ is the operator norm $\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{op}}$.

**Step 1: Reduction to a single unitary element.**

For $a,b\in U(V)$, set $c:=ab^{-1}\in U(V)$. Since $b$ is unitary,
$$a-b = (ab^{-1}-I)\,b = (c-I)\,b.$$
The operator norm is invariant under left/right multiplication by a unitary operator (because unitaries preserve $|v|$), so
$$N(a-b)=N\big((c-I)b\big)=N(c-I).$$
As $a,b$ range over $U(V)$, the product $c=ab^{-1}$ ranges over all of $U(V)$. Hence
$$\max_{a,b\in U(V)}N(a-b)=\max_{c\in U(V)}N(c-I).$$

**Step 2: Upper bound.**

For any unitary $c$ and any unit vector $v$,
$$|(c-I)v|\le |cv|+|v|=|v|+|v|=2,$$
since $|cv|=|v|$ by unitarity. Taking the maximum over $|v|=1$,
$$N(c-I)\le 2.$$
Thus $\max_{c\in U(V)}N(c-I)\le 2$.

(Equivalently, $N(c-I)\le N(c)+N(I)=1+1=2$ by the triangle inequality and $N(c)=1$ for unitary $c$.)

**Step 3: The bound is attained.**

Take $c=-I$, which is unitary. Then $c-I=-2I$, and
$$N(-2I)=\max_{|v|=1}|-2v|=2.$$
Concretely, choosing $a=-I,\;b=I$ (both in $U(V)$) gives $a-b=-2I$ and $N(a-b)=2$.

**Conclusion.**

$$\boxed{\max_{a,b\in U(V)}N(a-b)=2.}$$

The maximum is achieved, for instance, by any pair $a,b$ with $ab^{-1}=-I$, i.e. $a=-b$ (e.g. $a=-I,\;b=I$). Geometrically, this is the "diameter" of $U(V)$ under the operator-norm metric: two unitaries are farthest apart precisely when they differ by $-I$, i.e. when they act as exact opposites on every vector.
